brahmi.name: Brahmi
brahmi.summary: Ancestor of nearly every script in South and Southeast Asia, best known from the edicts of Emperor Ashoka.
facts: An abugida: every consonant carries an inherent /a/ vowel.
Other vowels are written as marks around the consonant, just like Thai today.

pallava.name: Pallava
pallava.summary: A South Indian descendant of Brahmi, carried to Southeast Asia by traders and monks.
facts: Many of Southeast Asia’s earliest inscriptions use it.
Common source of the Mon, Khmer, Cham and Javanese scripts.

old-mon.name: Old Mon
old-mon.summary: Script of the Mon kingdom of Dvaravati; later the basis of Burmese and Tai Tham.
facts: The Mon lived in the Chao Phraya basin before the Tai arrived.
Influenced some letter shapes of the Sukhothai script.

old-khmer.name: Old Khmer
old-khmer.summary: The most direct source of Thai script: the Angkor empire once ruled the Sukhothai region.
facts: Thai borrowed its consonant inventory and vowel placement from it.
Many Khmer words survive in Thai, e.g. เดิน (to walk).

sukhothai.name: Sukhothai
sukhothai.summary: Tradition credits King Ram Khamhaeng with creating Thai script in 1283, based on Old Khmer.
facts: Key innovation: tone marks (่ ้), which Khmer script lacks.
Vowels were first written on the same line as consonants, later moved above and below.
The authenticity of the Ram Khamhaeng inscription is still debated by scholars.

tai-tham.name: Tai Tham (Lanna)
tai-tham.summary: A separate branch from Mon, used mainly for Buddhist texts in the north.
facts: “Tham” means Dhamma.
Still used in temples and by Lanna cultural revivalists.

fakkham.name: Fak Kham
fakkham.summary: A northern variant of Sukhothai script, used alongside Tai Tham.
facts: The name means “tamarind pod”, after its curved strokes.

lao.name: Lao
lao.summary: Thai’s closest sister script, branching from the same Sukhothai line.
facts: Heavily simplified: dropped the extra consonants used for Pali-Sanskrit words.
Thai readers can often guess many Lao letters.

ayutthaya.name: Ayutthaya
ayutthaya.summary: Thai script stabilizes; the tone marks ๊ and ๋ appear in this period.
facts: The Chindamani primer (King Narai’s reign) is a famous early Thai grammar.
The three-class consonant system is codified.

modern.name: Modern Thai
modern.summary: Standardized with printing: 44 consonants, 4 tone marks, about 32 vowel forms.
facts: ฃ and ฅ remain in the script but are no longer used.
A 1940s spelling simplification was later reversed.
